stories.headline: Houthis strike Riyadh financial tower again and claim attack on Saudi refinery
stories.summary: Yemen's Houthis said they attacked the tower housing Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund in Riyadh and the Ras Tanura oil refinery, calling it retaliation for strikes on their territory. Eleven people were reported injured at the tower, the second attack on it in under a week. The group also threatened Saudi Red Sea ports, including Jeddah, while its fighters press toward the Yemeni government's seat in Aden.
stories.why_it_matters: Attacks on Saudi oil sites and its financial hub add risk to global oil supplies, which can show up in fuel prices, and the fighting around Aden threatens a wider humanitarian crisis in Yemen.
stories.background: The Houthis are an Iran-backed armed movement that has controlled Yemen's capital and much of the north for about a decade, fighting a Saudi-backed Yemeni government. Their attacks on Saudi Arabia resumed this autumn alongside a wider regional war involving Iran and the United States. Strikes have hit Riyadh's King Abdullah Financial District several times this month, including an earlier hit on the same tower on Nov. 19 that damaged several floors without injuries. On the ground in Yemen, the Houthis have taken much of the western coastline and are advancing on Aden, the government's temporary capital.

facts.text: The Houthis claimed attacks on Riyadh's financial district and the Ras Tanura refinery in eastern Saudi Arabia, describing them as retaliation for strikes on Houthi-held territory.
Eleven people were injured in the attack on the Public Investment Fund tower, the second strike on the building in six days; the earlier one caused no casualties.
Saudi Arabia's Civil Defence described the strike on the tower as a "terrorist attack"; at least two Indian nationals were among the injured and India's government condemned it.
A fire was reported at the Ras Tanura refinery, according to Deutsche Welle.
The Houthis said Jeddah and all other Saudi Red Sea ports would be targeted if Saudi Arabia attacks the Yemeni port of Hodeidah.
Houthi forces have advanced close to Aden, where Yemeni government troops are holding a fortified line; government forces said the Houthis will not take the city.
The Nov. 19 strike on the same tower damaged several floors and caused no injuries, and Saudi Arabia's foreign ministry said it reserved the right to take all necessary measures in response.

framing.note: Frames the strikes as a tit-for-tat cycle and stresses the cost to Riyadh's push to become a global business center.

stories.headline: Solomon Islands signs security treaty with Australia, barring foreign bases
stories.summary: The Solomon Islands signed a treaty naming Australia its primary security partner and stating that no foreign military or security base will be allowed on its territory. Several outlets reported that it sets aside the country's 2022 security pact with China, which had raised concern about a possible Chinese naval presence in the South Pacific.
stories.why_it_matters: The deal shifts a contest between China and the U.S. and its allies over Pacific islands that sit along key shipping and military routes. Right-leaning outlets in the ingest covered it mainly through the Telegraph's paywalled piece on China's setback.
stories.background: The Solomon Islands is a nation of about 700,000 people roughly 2,000 kilometers northeast of Australia. In 2022 its then government signed a secretive security agreement with China, alarming Australia and the U.S., which feared it could open the way for a Chinese military base. Prime Minister Matthew Wale, who took office this year, said in June he would review the China pact and agreed with Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese to negotiate a broad treaty covering security and the economy. This week's signing is the result.

facts.text: The treaty names Australia the Solomon Islands' "primary security partner."
The treaty states there will be no foreign military or security base in the Solomon Islands.
The Solomon Islands is setting aside its 2022 security agreement with China, according to the BBC and the AP.
Prime Minister Matthew Wale said his country would no longer be a point of regional uncertainty, the BBC reported.
Under the pact, the Solomon Islands will reject any foreign power trying to interfere with its sensitive infrastructure, Deutsche Welle reported.
In June, Wale announced a review of the China pact and agreed with Albanese to negotiate a comprehensive treaty with Australia.

stories.headline: China opens investigation into Shanghai party chief Chen Jining
stories.summary: China's Communist Party placed Chen Jining, Shanghai's party secretary and a member of the 24-member Politburo, under investigation for suspected serious violations of party discipline and law, state media said. He is the fourth Politburo member to be investigated since 2025.
stories.why_it_matters: Chen runs China's financial capital and was widely seen as a candidate for top leadership, so his fall signals how far Xi Jinping's anti-corruption drive reaches ahead of a 2027 leadership reshuffle. No right-leaning outlet in the ingest covered the story.
stories.background: Since taking power in 2012, Xi Jinping has run an anti-corruption campaign that has removed officials from local cadres to generals and members of the top leadership. Investigations announced as "violations of party discipline" usually precede expulsion and prosecution. Chen Jining, a former environmental engineer and president of Tsinghua University, became Shanghai's party chief in 2022 after serving as Beijing's mayor. The party is due to pick a new leadership lineup at its congress in 2027.

facts.text: State broadcaster CCTV reported that Chen is under investigation for violating party discipline.
The investigation is on suspicion of serious violations of party discipline and state laws, the Wall Street Journal reported.
Chen is the fourth Politburo member to be investigated since 2025.
Chen had been expected to take a top leadership role in 2027.
The case is the latest in Xi Jinping's long-running anti-corruption campaign, NPR reported.

stories.headline: Two Libyan officers die after Ukrainian drone attack on Russian ships; Italy objects
stories.summary: Two Libyan naval personnel died of wounds from a Ukrainian naval-drone attack on Russian vessels at Benghazi, eastern Libyan authorities said, and the Libyan army vowed retaliation. Ukraine said the strike was self-defense, while Italy voiced concern to Kyiv. In Ukraine, Russian strikes killed civilians in Zaporizhzhia and the Odesa region.
stories.why_it_matters: The war in Ukraine is spreading into the Mediterranean, near European shipping lanes and Italy's coast, drawing in Libyan forces and straining Kyiv's relations with European partners.
stories.background: Russia has built ties with eastern Libya's military leader Khalifa Haftar, whose Libyan National Army controls Benghazi, and uses Libyan ports for its ships. Ukraine has hit Russian vessels far from the Black Sea with naval drones; an analysis by the Center for European Policy Analysis counted three Russian ships disabled by drones in the Mediterranean over 12 months. In April, a Russian tanker was attacked off Libya by what officials described as Ukrainian forces operating there. Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine is nearing its fifth year.

facts.text: Ukraine confirmed it used naval drones in strikes on Russian vessels off Libya.
Ukraine said the attack on the Russian ships was self-defense, and its foreign minister described it as countering Russian aggression.
Two Libyan army personnel died of wounds from the attack at Benghazi port, the Libyan National Army and the head of eastern Libya's administration said.
The Libyan army vowed retaliation after the deaths.
Italy expressed concern to Ukraine over the attacks.
A Russian overnight attack on Zaporizhzhia killed two civilians and wounded 48, including four children.
A Russian attack in the Odesa region killed two people, including a teenager, local officials said.
Three Russian ships have been hit and disabled by drones in the Mediterranean in the past 12 months, according to a CEPA analysis.

stories.headline: U.S. jury convicts Huawei of trade-secret theft conspiracy and bank fraud
stories.summary: A federal jury in New York found Chinese telecom company Huawei guilty on 10 of 12 counts, including conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud, after a three-month trial. Jurors acquitted it of racketeering conspiracy and obstruction of justice. Huawei said it plans to appeal.
stories.why_it_matters: The verdict strengthens the U.S. government's case for keeping Huawei out of American networks and could feed into U.S.-China tensions over technology and trade.
stories.background: Huawei is one of the world's largest makers of telecom equipment and smartphones. U.S. prosecutors in Brooklyn charged the company in 2019 and later added racketeering counts, accusing it of a long-running scheme to take technology from U.S. firms and of hiding business in Iran from banks. The case led to the 2018 arrest in Canada of Huawei's finance chief, Meng Wanzhou, who returned to China in 2021 under a deal with prosecutors. Huawei has denied wrongdoing throughout.

facts.text: The jury found Huawei guilty of conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud.
Huawei was convicted on 10 of the 12 counts.
The jury acquitted Huawei of racketeering conspiracy and obstruction of justice.
Prosecutors also accused Huawei of doing business in countries under U.S. sanctions, including Iran and North Korea, and of making false statements to U.S. officials and banks.
The verdict followed a three-month trial in New York.
Huawei said it plans to appeal.

stories.headline: Colombian forces end Cartagena supermarket hostage siege
stories.summary: Colombian police and soldiers stormed a supermarket in Cartagena early Wednesday, ending a day-long siege by armed men who took shoppers and staff hostage after a failed attempt to rob an armored truck. President Abelardo de la Espriella said all hostages were rescued and one captor was killed.
stories.why_it_matters: Cartagena is one of Colombia's busiest tourist destinations, and the siege came a day after a car bomb in Villavicencio, adding to concerns about security in the country.
stories.background: Colombia has faced rising violence from armed groups and criminal gangs. President Abelardo de la Espriella, a right-wing leader, has carried out a broad crackdown on the drug trade. On Monday a car bomb outside regional government offices in the central city of Villavicencio injured 23 people. The Cartagena siege began Tuesday when an armored-truck robbery failed and the gunmen fled into a supermarket.

facts.text: The gunmen took hostages in a supermarket after a failed attempt to rob an armored truck, authorities said.
De la Espriella described the men as "common criminals" and went to the scene to take charge of the operation.
Security forces stormed the supermarket early Wednesday; the president said all hostages were rescued and one captor was killed.
The ordeal lasted about 17 hours, the BBC reported.
A car bomb in Villavicencio on Monday injured 23 people and destroyed a local governor's office.

stories.headline: Iran flogs singer Parastoo Ahmadi for performing without a hijab; UN objects
stories.summary: Iranian singer Parastoo Ahmadi and members of her production team each received 74 lashes over an online concert in which she sang without the mandatory head covering, according to her lawyers and local media. The UN human rights office called the flogging abhorrent and urged Iran to end the practice.
stories.why_it_matters: The punishment shows Iran enforcing its dress code on women with corporal punishment, a test of how far authorities will go against artists and protest symbols.
stories.background: Iranian law requires women to cover their hair in public, and women are barred from singing solo in public. The rules became a flashpoint after the 2022 death in custody of Mahsa Amini, which set off nationwide protests. Ahmadi drew wide attention in 2024 with a YouTube concert in which she sang in a sleeveless dress with her hair uncovered. Reports earlier this year said a court had sentenced her and her team to lashes.

facts.text: Lawyers said Ahmadi and members of her concert team received 74 lashes each in Qom and also face two-year bans.
Five people received 74 lashes each on Monday, local media reported, and the UN called the flogging "abhorrent" and urged Tehran to abolish the practice.
The conviction was for "outraging public decency" after she livestreamed a concert without covering her hair.

stories.headline: South African court sets aside Phala Phala report against Ramaphosa
stories.summary: South Africa's Western Cape High Court set aside in full the independent panel report that found President Cyril Ramaphosa had a case to answer over the 2020 theft of U.S. dollars from his Phala Phala farm. The ruling removes the basis for a parliamentary impeachment inquiry for now, though appeals are expected.
stories.why_it_matters: The ruling lifts, at least for now, an impeachment threat against South Africa's president and shapes the stability of the country's coalition government. Only centrist outlets in the ingest covered it.
stories.background: In 2020 thieves allegedly stole a large sum of U.S. dollars hidden in a sofa at Ramaphosa's Phala Phala game farm, raising questions about where the cash came from and how the theft was handled. A parliamentary panel set up under Section 89 of the constitution found in 2022 that he may have a case to answer, but Parliament voted not to proceed. In May 2026 the Constitutional Court ruled that vote unconstitutional, and Ramaphosa went to the Western Cape High Court to have the panel report set aside, winning an interim halt to the impeachment inquiry in July.

facts.text: The Western Cape High Court set aside the Section 89 panel report in its entirety.
The panel had found Ramaphosa had a case to answer over the Phala Phala theft.
Appeals against the ruling are likely, Daily Maverick reported.
The 2020 break-in involved thieves allegedly stealing bundles of U.S. dollars hidden inside a sofa at the farm.
In May 2026 the Constitutional Court set aside Parliament's earlier vote against the panel's recommendations as unconstitutional.
Ramaphosa filed papers on May 26 asking the High Court to set the report aside, and in July the court halted Parliament's impeachment inquiry pending its review.
